utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe there's something the parties would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's just one matter I'd like to raise. Your Honours, as indicated yesterday, we are racing very hard to have ready a witness -- sorry, a document list concerning this witness. Frankly, as the evidence unfolds, it may well be that that list becomes much shorter, and indeed I anticipate that is what's going to happen, quite frankly. So we have draft -- handwritten preliminary list, and Mr. Cengic is absent from court now because he's working on that very list. But what I would ask is that when the learned Prosecutor has finished the evidence in chief in this matter, we be permitted to have a longer than usual break for two reasons: First of all, to enable that list to be completed in a relaxed way, I think is the best way to put it; and secondly, to get some instructions on particular issues. Obviously for a long time this witness has been prepared with particular issues in mind. It may well be now that there are some documents that the learned Prosecutor has quite properly put to him and that may relieve us of the need to do that. And if we were granted that small amount of extra time, I think it would mean we'd be able to -- to provide a realistic list of the documents that we're going to use before we start, rather than doing it piecemeal. And secondly, I'm relatively confident that it would mean a much shorter cross-examination, quite frankly. We just want to wait until the end of this -- until the end of the evidence in chief before we make any decisions. So for that reason, I would ask the Court's indulgence for an extra 30 minutes of time to take instructions and to perform those functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask approximately how long do you need to cross-examine this witness? I mean, today is Friday, and we hope we could finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have said there was no chance of doing that, but there is now a chance of finishing him today, in my opinion. He was a witness through whom many of these documents concerning the investigation were to be put, as Your Honours might have inferred. Many of those documents were put to Mr. Gusic; many were put to Mr. Jasarevic. But the fact is the Prosecutor has also put some of those documents in now. It -- the situation is unclear, but it seems to me that there's a -- there is a possibility to finish him today, but I -- in order to do that, I really need to get instructions on particular matters. And as you know, we can't visit Mr. Halilovic in person during the week. You know, we can in afternoon sessions. But obviously this witness commenced yesterday. So I would ask for that time. But could I -- yes, could I say that normally I was planning for a little over a day of cross-examining for this witness, but I foresee that it will be shorter. And it may be much shorter than that, significantly shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I still note that next Monday we don't have the courtroom. The Appeals Chamber will take this courtroom for another case. So there's no sitting for us on Monday. If we did not finish this witness today, so that witness has to stay in The Hague for another four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I very much bear that in mind. If I could put it in these terms: The -- the witness gives evidence of some importance in the case, and I want to make sure I've got instructions that are quite clear on particular topics. But the substance of the instructions I'm going to be taking and discussing with Mr. Halilovic will be: Do we need to ask any questions about a particular topic? So it will be -- they'll all be designed -- or they'll all have the effect of potentially reducing, rather than increasing the time of this witness. And could I indicate this, too, Your Honours, that I would ask for that time of the extra half an hour because this witness has been brought forward in somewhat of a hurry to accommodate him. But if we should finish before that time was completed, we could of course advise the court deputies immediately and may be we could reconvene earlier than that time. And that is also possible, so that -- anyway, those are the matters that I have to raise, and I thought I better raise them at the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've -- we've got no objection to the additional 30 minutes of break time to -- if it can move the case along. I just wanted to know: Would this be an ex parte list that's being filed, number one? And number two -- since this list that they want to file with the Court, a list of exhibits, will this be an ex parte list? And number two, since the list is already finished, can the list be provided to the Prosecution if it's going to be provided to the registry and the Judges. Also, if there are going to be any long documents that we haven't seen, could we have the documents in paper form in English, because if there are going to be any long documents that are going to be introduced through this witness, we would then request some time to read the document, each document before they be given to the witness. We went through this problem in the last few weeks. I understand they don't want to produce their list of -- of their documents prior to the witness getting on the stand. But once he's on the stand, can they either provide us with a list or -- or once he's completed testimony, the list or the documents themselves, because the system is slow. You have to get out of the regular LiveNote, then go into the history, and then go through page by page. And if it's a long document, it's a very slow process. And we cannot be able to object or even analyse the document if we haven't seen it before. It's just going to slow things down. So we would ask that even though they don't have to provide documents ahead of time, when the witness is finished, give us the witness list, and if they're long documents and they're not in English, please provide us whatever they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not only reasonable in part, but it's one that was -- is the subject of ongoing discussions between the Defence and Prosecutors. So my learned friend is not raising it for the first time now. Discussions have taken place between myself and Mr. Re. Frankly, we understand the Prosecution position about the lengthy documents. There are no lengthy documents that are going to be put through this witness here. One might foresee some with Mr. Karavelic or with a -- or with an expert, so that in those situations we are going to work on some agreement that is viable for both sides but doesn't flout the spirit of the e-court. So in that -- with regard to the paper issue, there are discussions that should happen. As to the providing of a list, the list that's provided to the Court is confidential to the Court and not given to the Prosecutors because a decision hasn't finally been taken to use all of those documents. Some of them are just there to remind a witness in case he doesn't give a testimony. Sometimes the witness will say in 20 seconds, "Yes, this did happen." Then you don't need to waste the Court's time with a long document. So for that reason we don't want to be giving -- giving a list -- the list that the Court is getting to the Prosecutors in advance in the way that's being asked. And we don't believe that we have to do that. But in terms of embarrassing the Prosecutors with the -- with lengthy documents for the first time, there really is an issue about that because of the way that the e-court is slow to go between pages. And the Prosecutor is entitled to deal with that, I submit, on a case-by-case basis. But I do indicate to the Court, as Your Honour said, it's reasonable that something should be worked out. We are working on it and we are going to provide in some form access by the -- for the Prosecutors to those sort of things. Could I indicate actually where that discussion is up to now. We would prefer from the Defence side to spare us the need for work to release the document electronically but allow the Prosecutors to print it, to have a printer if the Court is happy for them to have such a thing in court so that they can print the document immediately it's released and then they can have it in hard copy. If that's unacceptable, if it can't be achieved, then it may be the Defence will agree to go and photocopy it ourselves and provide a copy to the Prosecutors. I'm being asked to slow down. That's where the discussion is up to the at the moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think the Prosecution was asking too much. It's just a list of the documents you used after the cross-examination of that witness. I believe it's a reasonable request. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And especially for those, you know, documents that you had your own source. It's not from the Prosecution but, you know, from your own collections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of providing a document -- a list of documents used after cross-examination of the witness, we see no objection to that being done at all. And the only reason why we don't want to provide it before the cross-examination is because, to keep freedom of action in relation to certain of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said "after cross-examination."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you mean after examination-in-chief? I mean, after our examination-in-chief, they provide the list of documents before cross-examination. If it's after cross-examination, that doesn't do anything for us. We still are -- I think that was a slip of the tongue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I said "after cross-examination."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If it's after cross-examination, we're still in the same situation. If it's -- we just need to see the document before they -- they question the witness because we're left at a disadvantage. We have to start looking -- we're going to have to ask for a break or a -- or time to reach each document before they ask the witness each -- any questions. That's how it's been done in any other case. If you don't want to give them ahead of time, at least when the witness is finished on examination-in-chief, you give us the list -- or give us a hard copy. We don't even want their list. When they ask a witness about a document, just turn it over to us. Just hand us a hard copy so we can look at it quickly. Other than that, we can't look on the screen to see what they're even talking about; quick enough to see what the document is. If it's a three, four-page document, we're at a disadvantage; we can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this Bench has already made a ruling on this issue already. I haven't seen any sufficient evidence for us to withdraw that ruling at this moment

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Secondly, this practice has been used in other cases before. We are not the only case applying this kind of practice. So there's no discrimination against our Prosecution in this case. Thirdly, this practice will apply to Defence in the future because when the Defence have their case in chief, they certainly will face the same problem as you do right now. Although there's a doctrine of equality of arms, but I think for the same practice the Defence is still in a disadvantaged position because of limited resources on their part. But anyway, we'll look into the practice and jurisprudence of this Tribunal for all other cases to see whether there's some way out for that problem. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, could we have on the screen, please, document D -- sorry MFI2626 -– 2266 -- 226. Examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, this -- the document I'm about to take you back to was one I questioned you about yesterday. It's the document of the 17th of September 1993 which was your report to Mr. Jasarevic, the one-page report about the information you had to that date collected about what had happened in Grabovica. Is the document on the screen yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that the date at the -- you'll see that the -- I just want you to comment on some of the dates. The date which you appear to have written or compiled the report is the 17th of September, 1993. I just want you to look above that, the very top right-hand -- sorry, left-hand side of the page. There's a date up there can you -- can you read that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first number is "8" -- "8", then "9". It's possible that it says "18" here. I assume that it's the 18th of September. I'm assuming that. All that you can see here is the number "8" and also at the top you don't see the letter "C." You don't see the letter "S." So some other letters from this document are missing, so I assume it that says the "18th."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And next is written "Subota," Saturday, and "07:08." What is that telling you, the writing across the top of the page on what looks like the 18th of September?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Communications centre of the Supreme Command Staff." This is the time when this document arrived at the communications centre of the Supreme Command Staff. It's at 7.00 on the 18th of September. It's 7.08. That's what I can see. And then on the right-hand side is the person who received the document and processed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move now to document D228, which was the last one we were looking at yesterday. Now, the document you were looking at before we broke yesterday was the letter from Mr. Jasarevic of that day, that is, the 18th of September. It's an order to you in relation to briefing him about what had happened -- or preparing a report on what had happened in Uzdol, Kriz, and Grabovica. Now, that's dated the 18th of September, that particular document.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you said a moment ago, does it suggest to you that he -- he sent this order to you before he had seen the report, which was D226, that you looked at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to that question. Apart from having an element of assumption in it, that -- well, that in fact wouldn't be a basis for objecting on it own because he's a professional officer and he'd be able to comment on that sort of thing, so I won't object on that basis. But the previous document showed that the -- it had arrived at the Supreme Command Staff. It didn't say that it arrived at the SVB, Mr. Jasarevic's organisation, so that although my friend points out that it arrived on the 18th at 7.00 in the morning, that's at the cryptographic section, it doesn't say -- it doesn't say anything about it one way or the other, I hasten to add. So asking the witness to comment on that basis seemed to factor in an assumption that the witness hadn't agreed to, that is that Mr. Jasarevic -- that that document would have gone to Mr. Jasarevic from that communication centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, maybe you could ask some questions to lay the proper foundations for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is -- I'll just say there is a difficulty when you can't show a witness two -- two documents at once and have him look at them in his hands and say, "Look at this one, look at that one, which one does it appear went first?" That's the -- the slight practical difficulty I have here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, what I'm asking you is there are two documents. Unfortunately you can only see one at the moment; that's the one which Mr. Jasarevic sent to you on the 18th of September, 1993. A moment ago you gave evidence and yesterday you gave evidence that you had forwarded a report to him on the 17th, and the document appears to have been received at the communications centre on the early morning of the 18th of September. From looking at the date of receipt in the communications centre, the time and date of receipt in the communications centre, and looking at the order that Mr. Jasarevic sent you, which doesn't seem to have a time on it -- sorry, the time at the bottom is 14.44 from the communications centre, my question is: Does it suggest to you that Mr. Jasarevic sent this report to you -- the order to you without having seen your report? Or does it suggest something else?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know. It's quite possible that Mr. Jasarevic did not receive my report when he sent it. It's possible. I don't know what the communications were like at the time. I really couldn't talk about the speed. It is -- my assumption is -- it's just an assumption -- that he did not have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we please move to document MFI229. There are actually two documents I want to show you basically at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that -- is it possible to do that and have the witness -- it's not. 229 and 230, both dated the 19th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One is an order and warning to Mr. -- from Mr. Jasarevic, and the other one is ostensibly your response on the same date. But if we can deal with the first one, which is D229. Did you -- have you seen that document or did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did receive it, yes. I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we please go to -- I want to go to 230.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I want to ask you before we do as we are, what was your response to receiving that document? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sent an answer, and you probably have it. Part of it was in a document of the 17th. And as for the other information, I was trying to obtain it, but communications were difficult. Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the bottom part of 229 is entitled -- the bottom half is entitled "Warning: You must immediately" - which is in capitals, the word "immediately" - request the submitted reports. If you are unable to submit the reports, your obligation is to inform the SVK of the reasons why you were unable to carry out the order, and so on. Can you comment on why Mr. Jasarevic would have phrased that to you in those terms?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on it, but that's my opinion. He asked that the report be sent immediately, and this is quite all right because the head of the security service had the right and he probably had obligations as the chief of the administration to ask for urgency. And then, secondly, he says: "You are unable to deliver a report," and so on. This is very broad. Reasons -- the reasons may be related to communication problems, to fear. All sorts of reasons. And finally, he says: "By this attitude toward the orders, you are making it impossible for us to carry out our obligations." This is to explain why he's insisting on urgency, and the obligations are, again, being spelled out. That's my comment on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a -- I think we can agree it's a fairly strongly worded at the bottom, because it's headed "Warning," and it says -- the last line says: "By assuming this attitude towards the orders from the SVK security administration, you are preventing us from carrying out our obligations towards the RBiH Presidency and the SVK." Now, implicit on that, I think we could agree on -- everyone in this Trial Chamber -- in this courtroom could agree implicit in that is a suggestion that there is an attitude on the part of maybe you or someone in the 6th Corps towards orders from the SVK, security administration. Now, was that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness can be asked a question, not have a proposition put to him like when it's evidence in chief, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe a direct question will be perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I was actually trying to get to the question. I'm saying if you assume that this is what it says and as a professional, I think everyone can agree that is in fact what it does say. My question is: Why would Mr. Jasarevic have come to that view and how did you view him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm ask that question first -- I'll ask that question first: How could Mr. Jasarevic have come to the view, if you accept the proposition that it appears he is of the view that his orders aren't being respected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just object again to the second part of the question. The question can just be asked simply: How could Mr. Jasarevic have come to that view? It doesn't need Mr. Re's comment attached to the end of it. That's -- that part saying that "if you accept the proposition," well, this witness is here not to accept Mr. Re's propositions. But the first part of the question is acceptable, and it should be kept to that. The witness can then give his answer to assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But I believe the more questions asked to this witness, the witness will get more confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, I'll withdraw the objection to that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, Mr. Eminovic: Accepting that Mr. Jasarevic appears to be of the view by that last line that his orders aren't being respected, why would he have come to that view?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic was the chief of the security service administration. This is neither the first nor the last warning of this kind that I received. He always insisted that matters be dealt with immediately. Here there was a problem. When I say "a problem," I am referring to, on the one hand, the impossibility of carrying out the obligations, the inability of myself and my service to respond with the urgency he insisted on. I cannot comment on the mood of General Jasarevic, who wrote this. I am sure he was under enormous pressure to have this done, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, I also was of the -- I had the feeling that this had to be done as soon as possible. However, he may have had the impression that I was presenting an obstacle. I don't know. But it's possible that General Jasarevic at the time did not have at his disposal full information as to the situation we were in. That would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what you meant by "the situation you were in" - that's at the time, that's the 19th of September - when Mr. Jasarevic sent that order and warning.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When referring to the situation we were in, I mean, first of all, our materiel resources and our possibilities. When you speak of a military security service, I think in the corps there were just two of us. At the time, there was another man who arrived but he was with us very briefly. He used to be a judge or, rather, he became a judge afterwards. So there were just two of us. We didn't have fuel. We were not able to go there ourselves on foot urgently. And all we could do was rely on what we had and perhaps collect information through means of communication. That was why the urgency that was requested could not be complied with. We had neither the human nor the materiel resources to respond with the urgency that such requests required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can document D230 -- MFI230 please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is -- is that document now before you, Mr. Eminovic? A document dated the 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your response to Mr. Jasarevic's order and warning?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my response. This is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a look at the top of the page. There's a -- a date, which isn't quite legible. It says: "93, Monday 13.20."

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that, as with the previous document, showing the time of receipt at the security administration communications centre?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just down the bottom of the page, there's a Main Staff of the Armed Forces stamp and a date of the 21st of September, 1993. Do you know what that -- do you know what that signifies?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the seal of the protocol the security administration. You probably know that the communications centre was in the Supreme Command Staff and the security administration was physically separate, so that communication was needed with reference to documents. And there may have been some discrepancies. In our work, all the documents that arrived went first to the chief, who initialled them. And quite a lot of time was lost in that way, in the communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to comment on a line in the second paragraph, the sentence that says: "We have tried on a number of occasions to do the job via other participants in traffic, but it has simply been impossible." Please explain to the Trial Chamber what -- what you mean by that, and in particular "participants in traffic," which is actually underlined on the document.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the sending of documents from me to the subordinate units, and the "participants in the traffic" refers to radio traffic. This means - you may have already heard this - when a document was printed out or typed out in Word, there was some kind of method of encryption used to pack it up, so to speak. And then it was sent on to another participant in the traffic. Sometimes the communications were poor sometimes due to weather conditions; other times due to the size of the document because the bigger the document, the more difficult it was for it to get through the means of communication. And very often during the war communications were hindered electronically. Those who had more powerful communications would somehow cover over the weaker ones and they were unable to communicate. Also, when there was a lack of electric power, then nothing worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about the situation as of the 19th of September, 1993 at the moment. Are you saying that those particular situations -- circumstances pertained then, or are you talking generally? A very brief answer to that one, please.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally. Generally. This does not pertain just to that date. There was a lot of activity at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then say that -- "Rest assured that this does not amount to our careless attitude towards UB orders but rather to the fact that it is impossible to communicate with Prozor in any way. Going there by motor vehicle takes six hours, and six hours to return, and literally there is not a single drop of petrol." I just want to ask you: Was that accurate, what you've written there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also have to point out that when the Prozor Independent Battalion is in question, they did not have electric power. They received it intermittently when they switched on the generator. When they switched on the generator, if they had fuel, then they would have electricity. The moment they switched it off, there was then less ability to communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was the effect of the generator being on or off with the ability to communicate with them? Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then the following would happen: You could communicate by short wave communications, because a short wave communication can be operated with a generator. These were only UK -- ultra short contacts, but you couldn't count on computer communication and packet communications because a computer cannot operate without the right voltage. This was a usual problem, not just on that day or the previous day; it was a problem that existed at all time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we please move to MFI D233.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to -- on the screen will be a -- an order from Mr. Jasarevic addressed to the 6th Corps command military security service and to Namik Dzankovic personally, dated the 21st of September, 1993. Is that a document you saw or received at the time, Mr. Eminovic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please scroll it down a little bit, please. Can I see the title of the page? Thank you. To be quite honest, I probably have seen this document before because in fact it was sent through me. I am referring to the security services administration in the 6th Corps sending this to Namik Dzankovic through me. This means that I received this document and I had to forward it on to Namik Dzankovic. I was supposed to pass it on to him, so it was sent through me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: Now, do you remember now, that is, in 2005, having received that document in September 1993 and doing what it basically says to do, that is, to send it on to Dzankovic? Do you now have a memory of having done so, or do you just -- or are you just saying that because it -- that's what it suggests you should do, that's what you think you would have done?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To forward the document to Namik Dzankovic? Well, I should have done it. There's no reason why I wouldn't have done it. I'm sure that I acted professionally with respect to every document I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told the Trial Chamber that you -- you thought the first time you had heard about what happened in Uzdol was when you received that order from Mr. Jasarevic, which was Exhibit -- or MFI228. And you've just explained that you -- that there were difficulties in contacting -- in establishing communications with the Prozor area and it would have taken six hours to get there by road and there was no petrol. What -- in brief, what steps did you and -- and/or Mr. Dzankovic, to your knowledge, undertake to find out what had happened in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- it's a compound question. It should be dealt with in steps. The witness can ask what steps he took, and the witness can ask if -- if he knows the answer to it, whether Mr. Dzankovic was asked to take any steps. To wrap it up like that in a compound question, in my submission, could lead to misleading, so I'd ask that it be broken up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the first part of the question is some background information just to let this witness to be familiarised with the situation and then the question comes up. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Eminovic, is: Just briefly tell us what -- what steps, if any, you, and Mr. Dzankovic, if he took any to your knowledge, undertook to find out what happened in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document mentions only the events in Grabovica, not the events in Uzdol. I'm referring to the document before me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just -- just -- pause there. I'm not referring to that document. Just -- I'm referring to one which I showed you yesterday, which was 228, but I'm just asking you about -- having received the earlier document, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness should be given the chance to see that document. He's been shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What do you mean by "the earlier document"? I mean which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 228. The confusion was the other document is just sitting on the screen in front of him. I wasn't actually asking about either document. I was asking him what he did. And he looked at the document which happened to be on the screen in front of him, which was a different document. That's the only confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the 228 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Eminovic, I'm not actually asking about the document which will appear in front of you. If you need to refer to it, please do. What I'm asking you about is what steps you took, or Mr. Dzankovic, if you know whether he took any, to investigate what happened in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is addressed only to me. I did not have to inform Mr. Dzankovic of it. I don't know what his obligations were with reference to Uzdol. These were my obligations. And as I said yesterday, I probably learned about the events in Uzdol from this document. It's possible, but I cannot assert that with any certainty now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is what you did. Mr. Jasarevic sent you this. What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used means of communications with the Prozor Independent Battalion, asking them to give me the information they had with reference to the events in Uzdol, because Uzdol was, I think, in Prozor municipality, so that it was within their area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you send it to, your communication?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent my communication to the assistant commander for security. It was very seldom that I sent anything to anyone else. When the service was in question, I could only communicate with the organs of the security services, not with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the name of the person you sent the communication to? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With reference to the Independent Prozor Battalion, there was a large turnover of staff. I wasn't always satisfied, because these were people who were simply not able to perform their duties properly. But I think in this case - and I cannot be absolutely sure - it was Bektas, Mustafa Bektas. If I'm wrong, please don't hold it against me, but I think it was either Muhamed or Mustafa Bektas. That's what I think now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without any explanation, can you just please tell me: Was it an oral or a written communication you sent to him? Just tell me whether it was oral or written.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we just talked about this communication. I'm almost sure that it was in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the assistant commander respond to your communication? And if so, was it in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was in writing -- no, I think I didn't get a reply. I think. But I can't assert that. It's very difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Independent Prozor Battalion was Enver Buza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive an account from him as to what had happened in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I did not get any reports from the commander. They always went up the chain of command and control. So the documents Commander Buza sent on would be sent to -- to the commander. This was an unusual form of communication -- would have been unusual, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out at the time had happened in Uzdol or what were you told, if anything, had happened in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. It's just brought to -- I apologise to my friend for intervening. It's been brought to my attention there that the interpreter may have missed a word after the word "commander." I would just it to be clarified whether the -- what the witness said, whether he said "commander" or whether he said "Commander Gusic." That passage is at page 23, line 24. I'd just ask for a clarification in regard to that from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The answer of this witness is: "As a result, I did not get any report from the commander. It always went up to the chain of command and control." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry. Just a team member indicated to me that they thought they heard the witness indicate the name of the commander. And we just want to clarify whether the interpreter heard that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe Mr. Re could re-ask this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, you heard the exchange just then. Did you say the documents will be sent to the commander, Gusic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The documents sent by commanders of subordinate units, reports, would go to the corps commander; namely, the commander of the Prozor Independent Battalion would send reports to Commander Gusic. That would be the usual channel of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out at the time had happened in Uzdol or what were you told, if anything, around that time that had happened in Uzdol as a result of your inquiries?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The unit comprising mostly -- for the most part- I can't say that it was 100 per cent like that- but mostly comprising of members of the Prozor Independent Battalion, perhaps numbering the size of a platoon or a little bit less. Perhaps I can make a mistake there when I'm talking about strength. In the course of the night, they went to the Uzdol Valley. They entered the valley. It's a valley, slightly larger valley accommodating several hamlets. According to what I know, in the morning hours they approached some building, a school or something like that, where there were soldiers of the HVO. That's when the conflict broke out. Fire was exchanged. Most of them were around the school. But as I said, the combat disposition was quite disrupted. After that - let's say when the exchange of fire started - there was chaos, which is what can happen in an inhabited area. There were houses with people in that area. There was intensive fire, shelling of that area. And then these forces withdrew. I think that there were some wounded. I don't know if anybody was killed or not. Well, they lost some of the equipment. That's more or less all that I have to say about that at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your information about who was in the village, that is, of Uzdol, when the Prozor Independent Battalion went there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Uzdol -- all I'm saying I'm saying based on some information that I had at the time. Uzdol is a territory which before this event and after this event was under the control of the HVO units. It was never the territory where the B and H army was. So all the information that came from Uzdol practically came from the participants, those who took part in this conflict, in these combat operations. Let me put it that way. According to what I know, they got to this school. Firing broke out after that. There was chaos, firing, pulling out, and so on and so forth, shelling and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what, if anything, was Buza saying about whether there were civilians or HVO people in the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buza wrote a combat report. I saw that report. To be honest, I don't know exactly when I saw it, but I did see it. Probably sometime later. I'm not sure. So please don't hold me to it. When other documents are in question, I'm not really prepared to say that I saw it a day before or a day after or a month before or a month after, but I did see the report at that time and he wrote that during the fighting in Uzdol. I don't know. They destroyed several scores of members of the HVO. I don't know the exact number. And I think - and this is the key to everything - they mentioned 30 armed civilians, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "armed civilians"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean anything. I mean if you want my comments, I can give them, but I think the best person to provide the comment would be Buza, because I don't understand the term "armed civilians." I personally don't understand what is an armed civilian, what's the difference between an armed civilian and a soldier. This is the issue. I know that our soldiers did not have uniforms. But as soon as they had a -- a rifle, then they became soldiers. I think that this is something that is very, very difficult to define.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence -- excuse me, your evidence yesterday was that a forward command post had been established in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think the terms used by the witness were that a forward command post had been established as far as he knew in Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, in Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Donja Jablanica, Mr. Eminovic -- I'll just go back and start my question again. Your evidence yet -- yesterday was that a forward command post had been established in Donja Jablanica and that it was the most senior officer at the forward command post -- the most senior officer at the forward command post was the Chief of Staff, General Halilovic, who was, in your words, "the greatest military authority there." What was your understanding from your professional experience of whose responsibility it should have been to investigate crimes that occurred in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: The responsibility primarily of the command, which commands certain units, or the commander who commands certain units, judging by this, according to my understanding, actually -- actually, we have here a whole set of circumstances and I have some new knowledge in relation to what I knew before, and so on and so forth. It's my opinion that all the possibilities need to be reviewed, everything that was undertaken by the top military authority at the time; namely, the commanders and komandirs of the units who were commanding those units at the time. And in my opinion, that's where the responsibility lies, in that chain, because we have namely a criminal act that was carried out; we have victims, casualties. We have perpetrators. All that is necessary is to establish the responsibility when we're talking about the line of command and control, and I think that's where the responsibility lies. I'm speaking this as a professional. This is something that is logical to me. I don't want to say that General Halilovic commanded that. I was just speaking on the basis of facts that I had at that time in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your last -- the last sentence: "I was just speaking on the basis of facts that I had at that time in that period." What I really want you to concentrate on, if you would, is that your -- of your understanding at the time, when you were in Konjic and there was a forward command post in Donja Jablanica, what was your understanding at the time of whose responsibility it should have been to investigate the crimes in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post. That was my understanding at that time in that period. That was my understanding of the problem at that time. That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Uzdol? Did you have the same understanding or a different understanding?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "did I have the same understanding," are you thinking of responsibility. Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You just said that it was your understanding that the forward command post should have had the responsibility to investigate the crimes in Grabovica. The question is in relation to Uzdol. Does -- is it the same, or did someone else, in your opinion -- professional opinion, have that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If within these activities which the forward command post conducted this, let's say, crime at the time was committed - at the time, we were not sure that that was that - if that was within the framework of that operation, then that would be the logical sequence. If an order was issued for implementation from one place, then that would be the logical sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's my examination -- that completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll have a break for an hour. We'll resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Eminovic. Just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, I would just like to address you for just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question by the Prosecutor is something that I would like to define my answer a little bit earlier -- over the break -- actually, I thought about it. My opinion when we're talking about responsibility for a criminal -- for the criminal act that was committed in September 1993 is that the responsibility lies in the chain of command and control and that it is necessary to establish the exact chain of command and control and based on that draw the conclusion about responsibility. Everything that I said stands; meaning that General Halilovic was the greatest authority and that at the time there was also the IKM, the forward command post. That's how I understood it at the time. This is all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Re, do you have any follow-up questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thank you once again, Mr. Eminovic. I just want to ask you some questions, first of all, on the topic of that IKM. You indicated that you at a later time saw it. Are you -- and you noticed that it was at Zuka's base at Donja Jablanica. Could I just ask you: At the -- at that time, how long after the -- the events, in particular the killings, was that? Was it one day or two days, or was it a few weeks later? Doing the best you can, what's your estimate?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. Could you please clarify it for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Look, I will. It's -- it's really a question concerning your knowledge of that particular IKM. Now, you indicated to my learned friend in questions that you'd heard certain things and that on one occasion that you went past it. And I just wanted to ask you -- well, look, perhaps I'll ask you -- I'll ask you some simpler questions. Pardon me. That was long, convoluted thing. Did you ever attend any meetings at the IKM concerning military operations in that area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And did you ever attend at that so-called IKM for any other reasons during September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at the IKM, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And did you ever go inside the -- the rooms where the IKM was said to be?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I ever go in there? Maybe later I did. I don't know. I really don't know. I did not go there at the time when this was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And you had no involvement yourself in planning any military operations in the area between Gornji Vakuf and Vrdi in September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just have to ask you a couple of questions, specific ones, about that. Did you ever see or were you ever shown a large map signed by Rasim Delic as commander in the top left-hand corner and by Sefer Halilovic as Chief of Staff in the bottom right-hand corner with the heading "Neretva 93" on it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw that map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And just finally on that topic: You took no part in discussions -- well, I'm sorry, you've really answered that question already, and I won't repeat it. Very well. Now, I just want to -- I want to ask you some questions about the situation of certain units in the 6th Corps in the -- in the weeks leading up to the said events. First of all, the military police units within the 6th Corps had been in existence for how many months? In other words, when was the 6th Corps formed, to the best of your recollection? And after that, how quickly did it get military police units?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Corps was formed in June. More serious work, however, started sometime in early July by the move to the building in Konjic, the Univitz building. That was the start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And how long after the move to the Univitz building were the two military police companies - one in Konjic and one in Jablanica - established?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police companies were actually military police companies. I don't know whether there was one or two. I think there were two. But they belonged to the former 4th Corps. In other words, most of the manpower by the formation of the 6th Corps were transferred to the command of the 6th Corps, but they already were in those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've indicated that -- in evidence already that the -- although the units had an establishment strength of 76 men, these two companies, to the best of your recollection, were somewhat under strength and were running at approximately 60 men each. Now, I just wanted to ask you something about that. Of the 60 men in each military police company, how many of those were in effect active policemen and how many were, if you like, support staff?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really -- well, let me try to answer that. Perhaps about 20 men a day were in a position to be actively used, from 15 to 20 people. Everybody else had certain assignments. That's more or less the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And the figure of 15 to 20 persons available on any given day, does that take into account that some people were on leave or were rostered off their shift, or should we subtract an additional figure from the 15 to 20 because of leave and rostered matters?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer this question. I can try to give you an answer though. If I say 15 to 20 people a day, I mean these to be people who came for the implementation of certain tasks. Some tasks are already planned the day before, so there would be 5 to 10 people who would be free there, free for other action. But I'm really giving you estimates. It's very difficult for me to talk about this. I really don't recall all of the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. But the estimates are still helpful. Very well. So just using the Jablanica company as an example. On any given day, a randomly chosen weekday, for example, you would expect to find 15 to 20 people reporting for duty on that day of which maybe 5 to 6 already had assigned duties. Now, is that a -- broadly speaking, is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be accurate, but it's an estimate -- a rough estimate. I daren't assert it with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I understand that. And could I just indicate, I'm -- I'm grateful to you for indicating when you're estimating. That helps us too when you state that. All right. Thank you. The 44th Brigade was a unit within the 6th Corps structure which was led by a commander named Enes Kovacevic? Does that accord with your memory?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And that unit was based in Jablanica and was sometimes called the Jablanica Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And who was the SVB chief in that brigade? Was that Mr. Sihirlic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the assistant commander for the security services for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter didn't catch the last part of your answer. Would you mind just repeating that -- that last part.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the assistant commander for security was Zajko Sihirlic, Zajko or Zajka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, was the 44th Brigade in the process of forming a company of military police? And by "at that time," I should ask you this: In late August and early September of 1993, was the 44th Brigade in the process of forming a company of military police?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a mountain brigade which according to the establishment could not have a company. It could only have a platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm sorry. That was a -- that's my mistake. Well, let me correct myself then. Was the 44th Mountain Brigade in the process of forming a platoon of military police in late August and early September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just excuse me one moment -- very well. I'm going to show you several documents now concerning the way these events unfolded. Some of them you may have seen before; some you may not have; some you may not recall. You are entitled to read them through, if you wish to. I'll take you to specific aspects of them. Just excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown -- it's an exhibit already admitted D153.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while this is being brought up on the screen, I just indicate this: What I'm about to show you is a note which seems to emanate from the 44th Brigade, and in particular from Mr. Sihirlic. It may be a document to which you've already referred in your evidence in chief, so I'll ask you to have a look at it and then you see whether it's familiar and whether it is indeed a document you've already spoken about or not.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you zoom in on this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to say I don't have the English version just yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just forgive me a moment, please, Mr. Eminovic. I haven't got the document myself yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Neither have I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have it. Does Your Honour have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no English version at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an English version. I don't know if the Prosecutors have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, just forgive us a moment, please, while we make sure that everyone has got the document in front of them. The Defence does have it now. While the technicalities of that are being sorted out, could I just ask you, Mr. Eminovic: Do you have the Bosnian version of that document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And are you able to see the whole document, or do you need it to be scrolled for you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be scrolled up a bit. I've read part of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, in relation to these documents, you're allowed to be proactive and ask for the document to be scrolled or changed when you need it to be. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, has that yet been scrolled in the way you asked?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just reading it now. Is there more text? Can it be scrolled a bit more?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. There's a second page. But perhaps if you scroll to the bottom of that first and then we'll ...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this page to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please have the opportunity to look at the second page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could it please be enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's just signatures here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the end of the document, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does it appear to you to be a letter from Zajko Sihirlic -- sorry, not a letter, a report sent to the 6th Corps Command military security sector at Konjic and dated the 9th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here. I did not receive correspondence of this nature, but that's what it says here on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- I wanted to ask you questions. It's not addressed to you personally, this document, I can see, but since it's 11 years ago or more that these events happened, I wanted to ask you: When you first found out about the -- the deaths or the potential for killings in Grabovica, was it because of -- of seeing this document or being told about this document by someone in your office? Using your memory to the best you can now.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I first learned about this from the commander of the Military Police Battalion, and that was orally through means of communication on the 10th. All the information that reached me -- well, it came through the corps command. I assume that this document arrived on the 10th or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my next question, that -- although it's dated the 9th of September, that doesn't mean you received it on the 9th of September, does it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you did see this document at some later stage, or are you able to confidently state that you've just never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether I saw it or not. If it was sent to me as a report, then I should have seen it and probably did. But what could have happened was that these reports were with my then-assistant, and he would summarise them, so I would not read the entire document in detail. That might have happened. However, I did have the possibility of seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand. Very well. Well, bearing in mind, and I understand it's very many years ago, but just to ask you a matter of detail: Did you become aware at that time, let's say the 9th or 10th of September, that some new camp inmates from the Dretelj camp had passed up the road and -- and had arrived in Jablanica that night? Or sorry, the night of the 8th and the 9th.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the camp inmates, I don't know. At that time, over a period of several days or maybe even weeks -- I can't recall -- please excuse me -- camp inmates arrived sometimes in large numbers, sometimes individually one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand that. I'm going to ask you some questions about the -- the various disasters which your organisation faced in the middle of early -- early on and in the middle of September, and I'll come to those in some detail in a moment. But before I get to that, I just want to take you to another document which you've already been shown by the Prosecutor and just ask a couple of questions about that. Sorry, just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the witness please be shown document -- it's MFI224.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document I'm going to show you is the brief note which you looked at yesterday from Jusuf Jasarevic which was addressed to you and dated the 12th of September, 1993. It will come up on the screen in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Okay. Thanks. Now, at that stage, I just want to clarify a couple of matters here -- the steps that -- that Jasarevic instructed you to take at that time were to take immediate steps to verify the information and document it, and to make an assessment -- carry out a assessment and make a proposal to the commander for the arrest of the persons who are the culprits for this crime, if one has been committed and, finally, to submit a report on these matters urgently to the SVK, Supreme Command Staff, security administration. Now, I'm not going to repeat the questions that you were asked by my learned friend about those documents other than to say that with respect to these instructions and with respect to all the instructions given by -- given to you by Jusuf Jasarevic, you tried to carry those out in good faith and to the best of your abilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were orders. I had nothing to say about it. These were my duties, my obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like the witness to be shown another document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is one I believe you weren't shown, but I'd just like you to have the opportunity to have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This document, Your Honours, is Defence -- sorry, this is a document admitted into evidence as D154.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just excuse me while that comes up onto the screen now. This is a document concerning Mr. Sihirlic again. And I'd just like you to have a look at it, first of all, and see if you recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's your signature, I take it, upon it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no signature here, but according to everything I can see here, it was my document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the text --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm making the grave mistake of proceeding from the English version there. I understand what you say. You mentioned to my learned friend Mr. Re yesterday in -- when you were asked questions by him that you had made some contacts with Zajko Sihirlic. And now that you see this document, is this one of those contacts that you indicated in evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And can I just ask this: Is the reason why you gave these tasks to Zajko Sihirlic in part because you were based in Konjic, far away, and because you had many other jobs that you had to do, as well as consider these matters?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me why? Am I supposed to comment on this? Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. No, sorry. Pardon me. It is a question. And I just wanted to ask -- I was asking you to -- to comment on why it was that you asked Mr. Sihirlic to perform the tasks that you set out in that order.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that Zajko Sihirlic was located in Jablanica and he was one of the closest members of the service to the Grabovica area, so he was able to get certain information. It would not have been logical for me to send this to some other brigade which was far away and not close to the source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The reference there -- I just want to clarify something in it. There's a reference on the second line of the English version, but it's in the first sentence. It says: "Take all necessary measures to shed light on the massacre of Croatian civilians in Dreznica. Identify the perpetrators of this heinous crime and obtain the documentary evidence for the whole case and report all findings to the 6th Corps SVB." I just want to clarify which crimes we're referring to. Although it uses the term "Dreznica," that's talking about the killings in Grabovica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You see -- by your leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was a lot of disinformation going around, and one of my tasks -- or this might have been an error, because Dreznica is nearby. It might be the same local commune. But I'm sure that this actually refers to Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're not disputing that with you in any way, and -- yes, well, thank you for that clarification. And with respect to that, the -- the tasks that you have assigned to Zajko Sihirlic are really tasks belonging to the pre-criminal phase of an investigation; in other words, not the criminal proceeding itself but simply the -- the pre-criminal or investigative stage. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my view, this is the pre-investigative stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And really --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents which constituted our daily communication, and then sent through closed channels. These are operative documents. They contain imprecisions. They did not then have the importance they have now. So if you find anything that is imprecise or not quite clear, you should not insist on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with my record in this case, let me assure you, I -- I won't. No, I'm grateful for that indication too, and we'll attempt to bring a realistic perspective to bear upon these -- upon these documents too?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender -- I offer that document for tender. Oh, sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me. I misunderstood. It is already in. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do you have the MFI numbers on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, pardon me. No, Your Honour. That was a slip by me. It is already tendered into the evidence as D154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. With the same MFI number on it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's already tendered, Your Honour. He made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, the Defence counsel has made a mistake, Your Honour. It was already tendered and, I think, accepted into the evidence. So it ceases to be an MFI number altogether. It went in -- it was -- it went into evidence through the witness Salko Gusic, I'm instructed, Your Honour. No, my -- the fault lies with me for attempting to re-tender it again. I simply forgot that it was in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. And the situation is the same with the document D153?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Pardon me. Thank you for that, Mr. Eminovic. The next document -- I'm showing you -- I'm not going to show you August of the documents that the Prosecutor went to before. I am just going to show you a couple of extra ones just to seek clarification about them, to the extent that you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, this next document will take a little time, and I shall explain what the process is. This is a document which has some handwriting on it by Defence investigators at a later stage. And because it's commentary about the case and is directly relevant about the case, we don't think it's appropriate to show that to the witness. What we've produced, therefore, is two versions of the document: One which has got the Defence annotations on it. We'll give that to both the Court and the -- and the Prosecutor. But it might seem like a prompt or in some way an influence or something that the witness shouldn't be troubled by. And he -- it was done after he -- the document had anything to do with him. So what we were going to do is show a -- a clean copy of the document to the witness and provide the copies which have got our handwriting all over it to the Court so that they know exactly what's being done. That's the course we propose to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it will be done in paper copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But what's the purpose for you to furnish us with a copy with the handwriting of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's just because that's the way the document appears on the -- uploaded, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We don't have to show it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's really just to have the -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have that clean copy first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sorry, Mr. Eminovic. It's -- it's an old document that we want to show you. And the reason for showing you this copy is because we wrote all over it ourselves and you don't need to see all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, the Prosecutor doesn't have it yet. While that -- those documents are being circulated --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just indicate to you and perhaps indicate to the Court as well: This is a -- a document that is -- we think it is, anyway, a direct carbon copy of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document that's being shown is -- in another form is already admitted as MFI225. But this version that we're showing the witness has got a piece of handwriting on it which we want him to comment on, so it's appropriate to deal with it separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you like me to call MFI225?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In front of you, do you have the -- a B/C/S document and in particular do you have a bit at the bottom which seems to be a note saying: "I am too busy. Namik, please take Zajko and finish this with him. Nermin." Do you see that passage? It seems to be under the words "Chief Jusuf Jasarevic."
