utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a note that you placed on this document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify. It's a document which through me was sent to Mr. Dzankovic, and I had the opportunity only to communicate with the assistant security commander at the 44th Brigade. Along with the document of Mr. Jasarevic, I just added the text that's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I just wanted to ask you a couple of questions about that. What is -- what is it that you were asking Namik to do and what was the role of Zajko to be in that, according to this note? In other words, what is it that you were asking Namik and Zajko to do here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: At the beginning of the text, it says, "Regarding the events in the village of Grabovica, a representative of the military security administration, Namik Dzankovic, and the" -- I can't read it now -- "in cooperation - excuse me - with the sector chief of the military security service of the 6th Corps will" -- I can't read what it says here exactly. But the point is that we are together to make a report, and the reason why I sent this remark at the bottom for -- is for Zajko to do this assignment instead of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's -- that -- good. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I tender that document -- or offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, my question is that: Is it the same document with the document MFI225?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's different, as I understand it, because it has the note to which this witness has attested, so it should be a different document altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know. Again, we have a difficulty. We have to pull up 225 on this screen and check it against the one on that screen. If Your Honour could just give me a moment to that. I can then indicate whether -- what our position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- the documents -- maybe if Your Honours pulled them up on your own screen, you could see the difference, if you retrieved MFI -- or D225. Your Honours can see that they appear to be the same text but in a different format. The Prosecution just -- just requires some explanation from the Defence as to why -- it could be that one is the received version and the other one is the retained -- or the other one is the sent version. But 225 has a large stamp and a signature on it. This one, the original of this one, doesn't have a stamp or a signature on it or the handwriting. Now, the handwriting is probably explicable, they say, by Mr. Dzambasovic, but that doesn't explain the stamp or Mr. Jasarevic's signature. They appear to be the same document but in two different copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Morrissey, do you have something to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't, Your Honour. I'll just have to be after inquiry made. My friend, I take it, is referring to the original Bosnian versions? Yes. Very well. Your Honour, look, I'll -- I'll have to have an inquiry made about that. Would you just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that the witness has already testified to the additional words appearing in this document and the contents of those two documents are the same, more or less the same. The only problem is the format. I think during the custody of the document there might be some different formalities. So taking this into consideration, we'll admit it into the evidence with a new number on it, but later on it is the Defence responsibility to find some explanations on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Your Honour, we'll -- we'll comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the new number for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: MFI268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you've been shown other correspondence already by the Prosecutor and other reports and taskings. There's one that I wish to show you now, which you may have seen before. You may not. You may remember it; you may not. But it is Defence 65 ter D573. Its ERN number -- sorry, now this document is MFI227.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it in paper form, 227? Well, it's not linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, I apologise for the delays. Sometimes these happen in the course of these documentary matters. Would Your Honours just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ERN number of this document is DD002797.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Eminovic, about that delay. Would you mind just having a look at this document now and reading it as -- at your leisure. And then I've got a couple of questions to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does that appear to you to be a document that was sent from Sarajevo on the 16th of September, 1993 to your service by Jusuf Jasarevic concerning events at Kriz and Prozor -- or Kriz, near Prozor? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to what it says here, this act was sent to me. Earlier on I said something that had to do with a different document that obviously happened before. You will have to forgive me, but I cannot sort out many things by date. So this is probably a document that I had and that was addressed to me, that was sent to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. And there are no tricks here. It's really for your comment that I offer this document, rather than to surprise you in any way. Looking at it now, do you have any specific recollection of -- of receiving that document? And in any event, are you able to comment on when that document arrived at your service?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. The document is clear. It's brief. I have no idea. My memory would have to reach very far, and it would be much better had I had all the documents in sequence. But obviously I will make a mistake here and there in dates, in the times, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me assure you that there's no intention to get you to make mistakes, and it's really your comments that assist the Tribunal here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could the witness please be shown another document. This document's admitted into evidence already as D149.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're going to be shown here is a document that appears to be a combat report from the Independent Prozor Battalion to the command of the 6th Corps. And I'm showing you this document because of the answers that you gave about where you got your information about Uzdol. This is a document I'm going to show you and ask whether this is one of the sources of information for your reports about Uzdol. When you see it, read it, and then you can answer those questions. And remember, while you're looking through it, you feel free to indicate when you'd like the page turned, or any other assistance.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll the document. Just a little bit, please. Very good. Thank you. Could you scroll it up a little more, please. This is a combat report which in principle did not come to me, so that I couldn't really comment on it. Perhaps I saw it. It's possible that I didn't. Possibly it didn't even get to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand in the normal course of events that would not come to you in your service as a combat report. But in terms of the sources on which you relied to compile your information, you mentioned the possibility, I think, of seeing a combat report. And I just wondered: Is this the combat report that you were referring to, or is there another document that you haven't been shown that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was another document, something perhaps that was at the level of the Supreme Command Staff. It was a kind of military information. As far as this document is concerned, I'm not sure. I really can't say anything. It's possible that it reached me. I cannot say that it did or that it did not. It's possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In preparing the reports that you did prepare for Mr. Jasarevic, you relied -- I take it you relied on what you were told by Namik Dzankovic and also Mr. Sihirlic and also other persons within your service who would give you information from time to time. Is that correct or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report are you thinking of and which events? Could you please be a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my apologies for that. Well, first of all, with respect to the Uzdol matters specifically, did you get material in relation to Uzdol from other SVB persons down the line, in the 6th Corps and also in the Independent Prozor Battalion itself?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Namik Dzankovic -- well, the information, how did they arrive? All that was relevant would be collected. I tried to establish such a relationship that the information that I received would be checked through the service. I did not give up on any single piece of information, but the only proper way was to channel them through the service. The reason for that was always to check the information. At the time, there was also disinformation, things like that, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned the disinformation before. And let me ask you a question about that now. Once you heard that there had been killings in Uzdol, did you become aware of reports in Croatian media to that effect?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian media? To tell you the truth, the media was not available to me. I didn't have access to the media at that time. I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I understand that. Now, turning to the Grabovica report that you sent. The information that you had there came from Nusret Sahic, from Mr. Sihirlic, and Mr. Namik Dzankovic; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive information from Namik Dzankovic. I wasn't informed by Namik Dzankovic. As for information that I did get, it came from Nusret Sahic, the commander, as well as the military police and the assistant of the service. Perhaps information did come that was given by Namik, but I didn't receive it directly. I got it from -- I mean, he didn't inform me. That was the relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It's correct to say that he didn't report to you in any line of authority and you didn't report to him in any line of authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would -- could be a correct answer. Although, in the seniority chain, he did have the right to ask me for certain assistance or help in accordance with the expert line relating to questions from the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I have a question for you just concerning the duty to investigate crimes. Leaving aside the question of who the particular commander was of -- well, I withdraw that question. When a crime is committed, it's the obligation of the commander at whose level that crime is committed to initiate an investigation by deploying his professional units to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the criminal act in question, whether it's about the unit, the individual, the service. But the obligation of the commander is to initiate, let's say, an investigation. That is his duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to your understanding, Namik Dzankovic was given the task of investigating the killings at Grabovica by Sefer Halilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know about assignment of tasks from the general to Namik Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll just ask you one question which might put an end to this line: Did you ever see the report that was -- that was provided by Namik Dzankovic dated 13th of September to General Jasarevic? Did you ever personally sight that report?"

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely don't know, because at that time I didn't see it. I assume that I didn't see it at the time. I didn't have the possibility to see the communication between Namik Dzankovic and the chief of the administration. Maybe sometime later, but I don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps later. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no recollection of seeing it; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, maybe I saw it and maybe I didn't. Until I see it, it's possible during the process of identification, let's say, of these documents with The Hague investigators in Sarajevo. Perhaps there I had the opportunity to see it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I -- I've got a different question to ask you arising out of these matters. Were you ever shown a document dated the 30th of August of 1993 by which Rasim Delic, the commander of the army, appointed an inspection team, including Sefer Halilovic as the team leader and Namik Dzankovic as the -- as the SVB security person?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you trying to ask me -- or to say did I see that document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, first of all: Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did see the document at some point, but much, much later, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have it in my hands much, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. Were you familiar -- did you know though that -- that Namik Dzankovic was in Herzegovina as the security member of an inspection team headed by Sefer Halilovic? Did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Namik Dzankovic, as a member of the military security administration, was in that team. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a document that's still on the screen. It's the combat report emanating from the Independent Prozor Battalion. Would you please look at the very top left of that document. There's some handwriting at the very top left. And I just want to ask you whether you're able to identify that handwriting. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness -- could that please be zoomed in upon so that the witness can see it closely.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay. I can see enough. This is definitely not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to identify whose it is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I can see, this is the handwriting of Aziz Kadic, my deputy. But I'm not 100 per cent sure. It's possible that this report the way it is, perhaps with some changes, was sent to the military security administration. It's possible, but I'm not sure. Why do I say that? Because of all of these scribbles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. It's really -- and look, I preface the question by recognising that it's a long time ago, but I'm really just pursuing what your sources of information were. And looking at that document and in particular that handwriting in the top left, do you agree that it's likely that your deputy explained the substance of this document to you, enabling you to make reports to General Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably the way it was. Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, the units who were based in Grabovica were actually sent back to Sarajevo on or about the 20th of -- of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but that would be that time. Whether that's the 20th or not, I really don't know, but that would be the time period. Perhaps the second half of September. I don't know if it was the last --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- third or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And I just want to ask you this -- a couple of questions about your knowledge of the inquiries and where that -- where those inquiries had reached at the time when the Sarajevo units went back to Sarajevo. First of all, during that time, did you ever have the name of one single perpetrator advanced to you by any of the people you talked to? In other words, was there a concrete suspect or more than one concrete suspect people who were named? And I'm talking now about Grabovica, not Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no name of the perpetrators in -- of the criminal act in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And furthermore, to your knowledge was there at that time -- well, I withdraw that. So far as the Uzdol investigation is concerned, all the information that you had after the inquiries that you made was that there was no crime committed in Uzdol but that civilians had been killed in the course of fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information that I had was that the crime could not be proved. I did not consider one or the other to be true or untrue. It was impossible at the time to prove what the truth was. You see, one of the problems of the service was always the following: Wherever you turned up, everybody avoided you. And so the story was closed. There was no information indicating that a crime had really been committed in Uzdol. It couldn't be proved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But in addition to that, you had positive assertions from the battalion commander that in fact no crime had been committed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the battalion commander was in question, this report was not a very serious one. Some of the statements he made -- well, I wouldn't like to comment on them. It might be best to ask him or if you can ask me a more specific question, I might try to answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I'm really just -- I'm not asking you to evaluate the truth or otherwise of it at this stage. I'm just trying to get a sense of what your -- what the information available to you was, and you've answered the question, frankly. Very well. As to the -- the Sarajevo units - I'm returning now to Grabovica again - as to the Sarajevo units, when they returned to Sarajevo, did you -- did the 6th Corps part of the SVB have the possibility to interview the soldiers who had been in Grabovica any more, or was that a responsibility that had passed over to the 1st Corps military security?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military security service and the Military Police Battalion of the 6th Corps was not able to interview the soldiers. And in my view, this should have been done within the units. You say the 1st Corps, the units from the 1st Corps ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to those units that went back to Sarajevo into the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know whether all these units were in the 1st Corps. I think the 9th was and the 10th was, but I'm not sure about the independent battalion or whatever its name was, whether it was part of the 1st Corps. Probably it was, but I'm not sure. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. I won't press you if you don't know about them. But at all events, all of those units that -- that were part of the 1st Corps, upon returning to Sarajevo, they could be questioned by the SVB of the 1st Corps but not by the SVB of the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in short - and I'm just going to summarise now, if -- if I can, and you tell me if this is accurate or not - the SVB -- sorry, during the time when those Sarajevo units were in Herzegovina, the SVB performed a number of tasks. And I'll list them. The SVB sought information about the crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SVB considered the possibility of a site inspection but established that it was impossible and dangerous to conduct that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SVB considered the possibility of interviewing soldiers but was unable to do so because the soldiers were involved in combat activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the same question as you asked before. What I'm trying to say is there was no possibility of interviewing soldiers who were involved in the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, after less than two weeks had passed after the crime, the soldiers from Sarajevo left the area of operations of the 6th Corps and, therefore, of the 6th Corps SVB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that Namik Dzankovic was corresponding with and meeting with members of State Security Services and the civilian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I assume that's correct, but I didn't have any knowledge of it. It's possible that he had those meetings on the ground, but I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you at all times held yourself out as ready and willing and able to help Mr. Dzankovic in any way you could during the course of those two weeks or 12 days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty. Yes, I was ready and willing, and ultimately it was my obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it might be appropriate to take the break now. Can I indicate I think it highly likely that we'll complete this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me how long do you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I want to consider that on the break, but I'm -- perhaps I have only three documents that I propose to put to him from here, but there are some other questions too. That's the ambit of what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For Your Honours' planning purposes, can I indicate that on present indications I have two questions I wish to ask in re-examination following my learned friend's cross-examination, because, of course, we have to factor that in as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll try our best to finish the testimony of this witness today. And during the break, I will get in touch with the registrar to see whether there's any possibility for us to have some extra time this afternoon. Is it agreeable to the parties if we seek some advice in this aspect from the registrar? Which means, do you agree that we sit this afternoon? I know it's a Friday afternoon. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we agree, if needs be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 1.00, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a matter I would -- just excuse me please, Mr. Eminovic, for one moment. Your Honours, I have an explanation now relating to the differences between those two documents. It just might take a few minutes to explain it. Now, I can deal with it attend or -- in order not to waste the witness's time now, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It might be best to complete the cross-examination. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Eminovic, in the break, the length of time of the questions has shortened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So I can now ask the witness please be shown in a paper version -- this is ER -- sorry, Defence 65 ter -- and it would be MFI269. And Your Honours, we'll ensure that this is uploaded appropriately in due course. Sorry, Your Honours, I can just indicate the reason this was in paper is there was a mistake in the scanning. It was meant to be uploaded. It's actually got an ERN number but it hasn't been uploaded because of a scanning glitch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned earlier on in the cross-examining that you had a number of problems in the 6th Corps quite apart from -- quite apart from what was happening in Grabovica. Does this order relate to some problems occurring in the village of Lisicici - I'm sorry, I really don't know how to pronounce that one - but Lisicici? Were there problems with some specified Arabs in that village to which you responded in this order?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment on this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Yes. I'm inviting you.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a group of about 10 foreign nationals. I assume they were Arabs. And this group had 5 or 10 men at the most. They were in the village of Lisicici, which is on the right bank of the lake opposite Celebici. They were causing problems. On several occasions, they had taken a vehicle belonging to the European monitors. I think that they had stolen a vehicle from the European monitors. I'm not sure exactly from whom. And this was done pursuant to an order from Commander Delic. The corps command had received an order from Commander Delic that we were to solve this problem with the Arabs stealing vehicles and so on and so forth and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- before this, I went to that village and spoke to the leader of that group. I had an interpreter with me, a man who spoke Arabic quite well and who was a member of the 6th Corps. And I told them they should not cause problems, that they should not hinder anyone, things to that effect. And I told them I would use force if they continued causing problems. And this was an attempt -- after my warning and my order, they restored the vehicle. It was a jeep. I think it was a Mercedes with dark glass windows. I can't say exactly when, but I know that they left area of responsibility of the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that explanation. And I just wanted to ask you: I noticed that your order was directed to Nusret Sahic or Sahic, and I wanted to ask you how many of his troops of his company of military police was he planning to use in that particular operation to get -- to get rid of these troublesome visitors.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I couldn't say. This was an order drawn up as follows: As I said, there was an order from Commander Rasim Delic saying that they were to be deprived of their liberty and that the vehicle was to be returned. As there was no commander there at the time, I did this, and thank God this did not have to be implemented. In the meantime, matters were wound up. They were -- they were completed in a lucky manner, a fortunate manner. Otherwise, we would have had to draw up a plan in connection with this order. But this was never done actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my comment to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what's the relevance of this document or this piece of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I fail to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's just to illustrate the other pressures that were on the service. The Prosecution -- well, I've been counselled against making these comments, so I'll restrict it to this: The Prosecution make an allegation of inactivity, effectively, and I want to establish that the forces that were supposed to -- or that could have been deployed in the theory of the Prosecution had a lot of things that were on their plate, including this particular incident. And that's why we say it's relevant in quite a direct way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. The Prosecution agrees that it actually supports the Prosecution case because if it shows that the 6th Corps or the military police were able to investigate some matters; our case is why couldn't they investigate the more important ones, such as Grabovica. So we welcome the tender of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since there's no objections from the Prosecution, this document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: With a number pronounced by the ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have another document to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown MFI236.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document which is about to be shown to you may be a document of yours, and I'll ask you to -- to confirm whether it is or not when you look at it. It's addressed to Jusuf Jasarevic in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if the witness could just be shown the final page first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, I'm just show you the final page to see whether -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's only one page in Bosnian. I apologise. So could the witness just be given the chance to look at the bottom of the page quickly and then also the opportunity to read the -- the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it may be sometime since you've seen this document, if indeed you've seen it at all in recent times, so feel free to take time and then I'll ask you some questions about it, whether it's your document, and so on.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Let me just ask you some questions. First of all, is that your -- does it have your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well, I wanted to ask you about this -- this topic. Is there -- is your name there on it? Do you see the name "Nermin Eminovic"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, assistant commander for intelligence affairs has been crossed out, and in the heading -- this is actually a report which arrived from the assistant commander for intelligence affairs, which probably reached our assistant chief of staff for intelligence, and he probably copied it and gave it to us in view of the information the document contained. As far as I can see, the handwriting is the handwriting of my then-deputy, and this in fact represents our preparation. We only had one computer, which was encrypted. So he simply put this text -- he scanned it and prepared a report for Mr. Jasarevic. This is an operative report. It's one of those. It had no intention of being the most precise and the best document. It simply contained all possible information that could be gathered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You just gave an indication of the assistant commander for intelligence -- oh, sorry. Pardon me. I withdraw that. You've just indicated that this document probably reached your assistant chief of staff for intelligence, who probably copied it and gave it to you or to us -- "to us," I think was your term. What's the name of that person to whom you're referring, the assistant commander for intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. Just a moment, please. I didn't see this before. It says here in the heading: "Security sector." So this was then sent to me, but it was sent by the intelligence officer. This was unusual at the time. This is an unusual kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just -- sorry, now, just -- it's my fault, perhaps because of the way I asked the question, but could you just explain what the -- what has happened with this document, where it appears to have been written and how it appears to come to you. Can you just explain that. I know you already have in some respects, but I was confused by it, ask so I'd just ask if you wouldn't mind taking us through that once more.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the Independent Prozor Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to the security sector, as it says here. It was signed, it says here, by the assistant commander for intelligence, and an intelligence officer sending such a document to me was an unusual thing to happen. This was not what normally happened. But this probably happened because we asked for as much information as possible about the events in Uzdol. Maybe that's why he sent it. And this probably then went to the security services administration, as it's addressed -- as it's addressed the way it is, I assume that it ended up in the administration, but I cannot assert it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But by the markings on it, that is the appearance it has; correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's the case. This is my language, and I understand this. I also know the methods of work at the time. However, it's possible that the text we see here was somewhat revised when this was sent. Something might have been corrected or added. It might have been amended a little. Maybe it wasn't sent in its entirety, but maybe it was. I really don't know. You would have to see what the final document looked like. I think that most of this text went to this address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So in conclusion, this appears to be a draft document to be sent on to someone else at a later stage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could probably be the best definition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Okay. Well, I have some questions about the -- about the information contained in it, and I'd ask you to exercise your memory the best way you can and see whether you can recall what you knew about some of the -- some of the information contained in it. First of all, was it operative information known to you at the time that "bus driver Slavko Mendes was captured during the Uzdol attack and sent back with a demand for the others to surrender as soon as the driver approached the school and passed on the army's demand. Someone from the school shot at him through a window and killed him and fierce fire was opened." Now, was that operative information that you can now recall?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory doesn't help me much here. This is an operative document. I really don't know -- don't remember. In my testimony earlier, I said that considerably -- I gave a much smaller number of participants in the combat than it actually was, just because I really didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. All right. I have just want to move on to the next -- the next issue. Was it within your knowledge at the time, according to operative information that existed, that most of the Croatian soldiers were in private homes, "So they opened fire at our men from the houses. The fire was returned as much as possible at that proximity"? Was that operative information known to you at the time; namely, that there was a fierce battle involving shooting at and from private houses in the Uzdol area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's stated in the text here or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's stated in the text. Perhaps -- in the Bosnian version, it's about 10 lines from the top, near to an underlined section.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does -- do you recall whether that -- I'm sorry, I cut --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this is one of the reports that I did receive. The real truth is something that only God knows. This was given to me as one of the reports which should have been relevant --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and so on and so forth. It's very hard to say what the actual truth is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand you had an obligation to pass on operative information, whether it was true or not true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not whether it was true or not. If I knew -- I mean, it was my obligation to send on information that was as true or as correct as possible. The intelligence service and us were expected to have the most precise and the most reliable information at our disposal. This is the precision and reliability to the extent it was possible to have at that time. It's not just my job to pass the information on. I also need to check whether it is correct or not. At that moment, I didn't have the means to check this information, because it was coming from a certain source and it wasn't possible to check it for veracity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not able to go to the village of Uzdol or the hamlets within Uzdol because they were back under HVO control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was under the control to have HVO all the time. At the time, we called it "temporarily captured territory."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One other matter I just wanted to raise: Probably about maybe four or so lines from the bottom, there's a reference to -- and I'll just read you a sentence: "In -- in such a lightning action, there was no time for either looting or mutilation, as the Croatian media are trying to portray it." And then there's a reference to: "There is an example where our soldier hid women and children in a basement in order to protect them from the shells. This was also confirmed on Radio Rama in an interview with one of the women, except that it was added in a commentary that he had done it for money. Even the exact name of the soldier was mentioned." Now, I just wanted to ask you about that. Having seen that -- that paragraph, can you now remember anything about HVO media reports, Radio Rama, for example, or other such outlets? I mean, I appreciate it's 11 years ago, but I just ask you to extend your memory as much as you can and see whether you can recall anything about the coverage of these events by the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell the truth, I didn't have the possibility to communicate, to find out what was going on or being reported in the media at the time. It was the task of the intelligence service. It was their duty to monitor and to gather information from the other side. Let's put it that way. So this -- in view of the fact that this was sent by an intelligence person, then that's probably it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Just in thinking back, do you recall the story independently of a soldier from the -- from the Bosnian army side sheltering any civilians in a basement? Do you remember that or -- that story or not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer -- I'm sorry, it's -- I don't offer it. It's admitted already. Thank you. Very well. Just excuse me. All right. Well, I'm now into the last -- the last questions. And they're going to be very short now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, do you recall that an operation called Operation Trebevic III took place in your area, in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't need to know the exact dates, but I take it that took place after Operation Trebevic took place in Sarajevo on the 26th of October, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan for the action was drafted sometime in November. It was sent to the military security administration. I think this was at the end of November. And then it was sent to the administration for verification. And I think that's when it happened. To be honest, I think that some actions had already started which could have been implemented before the actual plan itself. I don't remember exactly when the plan was signed, but the implementation, I think, was in January. I can be wrong, I think, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, now, I'm not asking you for a full summary of the -- of the actions in Trebevic III, but I just wanted to ask you one question about it, that is: Did the Trebevic III operation that occurred in the Konjic area have any relation to the crimes committed at Grabovica or at Uzdol, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - I can be wrong here, but - when we're talking about Grabovica, the charges were drafted against unidentified persons. But really I can't be certain. As far as Uzdol is concerned, if I remember correctly there was no work done on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, thank you for your patience in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That is the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. It seems to me that we could finish the testimony of this witness in the morning sitting. Yes, any redirect examination, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is. Can Your Honour just excuse me for one moment. I'm just looking for a transcript reference in relation to the last answer. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, my learned colleague Mr. Morrissey questioned you about an order on, I think it was the 14th of September, 1993 involving an investigation into activities by "Arabs," foreign nationals, you described them as. Do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be clear here, in my conversation with them I, around the time when this order was written - I think before or after; don't hold me to it, I really don't know - I tried to get in touch with them. I had a person who spoke Arabic perfectly, like I said. To the question where they were from, they would say, "From Islamija." Islamija doesn't exist as a state. And then I would ask them, "Why are you doing this?" And then they would say, "Well, there, we just want to be doing this. You don't want to fight," and so on and so forth. So then I asked them, "Would you be able to do this in your country without being punished," and then one of them said, "No." But name, last names --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was only asking you whether you knew where they were from. Now, my next question to that is: Were they -- do you know whether they could be classified as "Mujahedin"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were armed. All right. Let's say that it was a group -- well, very roughly, but "Mujahid" in the Islamic interpretation is a broad term, and it's more or less "a fighter on God's path." They were armed Arabs who were staying in this territory, so that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the names, last names, we didn't know. I also know that they themselves did not have their passports on them. They kept them in places that were -- possibly they had several passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was, for the record, Exhibit D269.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, in cross-examination Mr. Morrissey asked you about the feasibility of interviewing those who may have been perpetrators at Grabovica, and your answer was: "There was no possibility of interviewing the soldiers who were involved in the crime." When you answered that question from Mr. Morrissey in the indirect phrase of "there was no possibility of interviewing them," were you referring to yourself specifically or to other people, such as Mr. Dzankovic, the military police, or -- or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking of myself. I was thinking of the service of the 6th Corps. And I also was thinking of the military police. This is what was being talked about. Nothing else. And concerning Mr. Dzankovic, I assume that he also was not able to have these interviews. It's my assumption. I'm going to be sincere now and say that at that time each one of us who would try to approach those people by force would -- would get a bullet, roughly speaking. I mean, I don't know, but they would have problems. They would have problems. Maybe I am speaking roughly, but don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was that last answer you gave about getting a bullet, was that based upon an assumption or personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about assumptions, not any knowledge. Perhaps I was a little bit hasty earlier using the vocabulary from before. But there, in any case, let me correct myself. I wouldn't be able to get a statement. Ultimately, I would be chased off. You couldn't really do this very easily at that time. I am speaking this as an assessment based on general information, nothing precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally - thank you, Mr. Eminovic - my learned colleague Mr. Morrissey asked you about the Uzdol -- what he called "the Uzdol investigation." His question was: So far as the Uzdol investigation was concerned, all the information was that no crimes had been committed but that civilians had been killed in the course of fighting," to which you responded: "My information was that the crime could not be proved." In relation to that proposition he put to you and your question, my clarification -- my question of clarification is: What was your professional view as to whether a -- I withdraw that. You gave some evidence yesterday about investigations into other possible crimes, and you specifically mentioned "smuggling and contact with the enemy and the investigations your -- the military police carried out." In relation to the investigation that Mr. Morrissey suggested may have been carried out in relation to Uzdol, what was your professional view as to whether a proper investigation had actually been carried out into the Uzdol crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've got an objection about that. It needs to be specified whether he's asking -- whether my learned friend is asking whether now he thinks a professional investigation was carry out, with the benefit of everything in hindsight, or whether at the time -- whether the question relates to the time. Because at the time the witness hasn't agreed that crimes -- that he thought that crimes had been committed. He's given evidence so far, and frankly my question was about the information that he had. So that's the -- my friend has to clarify what he's -- what opinion he's asking for here before that question can be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is -- and I apologise if it's not as precise as it could be -- is directed to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if that's the case, then my question upon which my friend is re-examining was a question about what was his information. That's not an invitation to have an opinion. So -- but frankly, in order to assist matters, I won't object to the -- the simple question being asked: What was his opinion at the time? Whether he knew the offences had been committed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go along this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. But the question -- I read the question out completely, which was: So far as the Uzdol investigation was concerned ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Eminovic, do you understand what I'm saying to you or do you need it clarified after that exchange?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please clarify it, because you have been communicating a lot now, so I don't know what the question is any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey proposed or suggested to you - I'll read the question to you again so you know exactly what my question is - he said to you: "So far as the Uzdol investigation was concerned, all the information was that no crime had been committed but that civilians had been killed in the course of fighting." Your answer was: "My information was that the crime could not be proved." Yesterday you gave some evidence about investigations carried out by the 6th Corps into criminal activities such as smuggling and contact communication with the enemy. My question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene again, but a simple question should be asked here. It's re-examination. It's not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I please explain. I've -- I probably could have got through this much more quickly by now. He gave evidence yesterday of investigations, which he said were carried out at his behest. Mr. Morrissey asked him about an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- also put words into his mouth about an Uzdol investigation. I'm asking him to compare to two as to whether the Uzdol one was a proper one in terms of the investigations he'd seen carried out so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could just put a very plain question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the context of investigations that you had seen carried out before, such as those you described yesterday - smuggling, contact with the enemy - and in the context of the question, Mr. Morrissey asked you about the Uzdol investigation. At the time, what is your view as to whether there had been a proper investigation into the alleged crimes at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object again. Now the question is: What is your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your view - I'm sorry - at the time. If there's any dispute as to whether it was now or then, I'm only referring to then. And I do apologise because I have to lead it back to the question he was actually asked.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigations are being talked about here and information. An investigation is based on information. I cannot start an investigation without information. So the information I receive for each investigation is something that I receive from the service or from the police, and then based on this information, which we had at our disposal at the time, you could not have evidence that a criminal act had been committed. It was a question whether it had happened at all. If I understand what was being discussed here and try to -- I can try to answer in this particular way. Or you could ask me -- maybe -- maybe it's a question of language also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking you is -- is just this: You said yesterday that there -- you had had some investigations into activities -- criminal activities by the 6th Corps. Today Mr. Morrissey asked you about the Uzdol investigation.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: What was your view as to whether a proper investigation had been carried out in relation to the Uzdol crimes, compared to the investigations you had seen carried out in relation to other crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about Uzdol, an adequate investigation - perhaps this is what I think now - could have been carried out had certain information been available which was not available at the time. I say "perhaps." From this point in time I believe that. But as far as other investigations are concerned, which you mentioned, they were in the terrain which we had control over, in the physical sense, and it was possible to carry them out at the time. I mentioned smuggling. But what we're talking actually is -- what we're talking about actually is the following: A kilogramme of tobacco, it was known that the price for that was 400 bullets. That was the price. For one lamb, you could get 10 shells. So these were the prices that were current at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Finally, at page 58 of today's transcript, Mr. Morrissey, my learned colleague, was questioning you about the report of Enver Buza, and you said -- the question was: "In addition to that, you had positive assertions from the battalion commander that in fact no crime had been committed; is that correct?" Your answer was: "When the battalion commander was in question" -- I think in question -- "this report was not a very serious one" -- was in -- "some of the statements he made -- well, I wouldn't like to comment on them. It's best -- may be best to ask him." My question is: What did you mean by saying "this report was not a very serious one"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that the person who writes "30 armed civilians" must define such a term. That's the lack of seriousness in that report, not the mention the numbers that are referred to there. They are very, very - how shall I put it? - imprecise, given off the top of one's head. These -- this is -- these are my thoughts about that, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there still any documents from the parties to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution. They are all tendered, I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, MFI268, we seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the document that was distributed in paper copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This was the one Mr. Morrissey was going to provide the Trial Chamber with an explanation about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that the one? No, I don't think it's that one. I think that one is about the Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the -- I think -- I think the -- the guests -- the Arab people was 269, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And this one is 268, and the comparison between MFI225 and 268 is the matter that -- that the Prosecution raised. And having the documents in front of me now, I can see what the issue is. 165 appears to be the original, and then what may have happened -- and it may be that I can lead this evidence -- if the witness listens to the explanation, then if there's any difficulty, we can ask him about it. What appears is that 165 is a document stamped and signed by Jusuf Jasarevic, and that appears to have arrived at the 6th Corps. It looks as if it's then been re-typed and it's in a different typing format, as the Prosecutor correctly identified. It's then written that it's Nacelnik Jusuf Jasarevic at the bottom, but there's no signature apparent, so it looks as if it's been re-typed. Thereafter, you get the note that this witness indicated he'd appended to it, and it would appear that that's the copy that was sent on to -- I'm sorry, I don't have the English version in front of me now, but that would appear to be the -- the copy that was sent on to Dzankovic and which indicates to Namik, "Please use Zajko to assist." That's the way we -- that's what we think is the -- that's what we think the -- the explanation is. I'm happy -- well, I can ask the witness about it. If the Prosecution wants me to pursue it further with the witness, I can. It might take some time, but it can be done, so I can provide -- I've got hard copies. I can pass my copies over to the Prosecutor so they can inspect it -- oh, they've got it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, do you have any comments on that, since this document has already been admitted into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I don't. One has been admitted. The other one, they were seeking to admit into evidence, the second one. The witness has provided an explanation. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence. Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We managed to finish your testimony today, and Madam Usher will show you out of the room and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there anything else the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- could we just place on record appreciation for the court interpreter service in assisting us to finish this witness in the way that has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. I believe you have taken the words from my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution also likewise expresses its appreciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll resume next Tuesday. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
